[3] Some libraries, like Java, may notify the application once per time the subscriber gets behind rather than on every dropped message. This approach helps mitigate the noise of frequent notifications. Additionally, libraries may offer a way to get a count of dropped messages, allowing applications to detect and respond to issues.

To handle these dropped messages, several patterns are available:

[3] One common pattern involves buffering incoming messages for a subscription. This allows the application to process messages at its own rate, maintaining the appearance of a healthy connection to the server. When the application is not able to process messages fast enough, it will drop messages to keep the connection healthy.

[3] Another pattern is for the client to notify the application when there is a SlowConsumer error. This notification occurs when the client detects a slow consumer locally, allowing the application to take appropriate action, such as handling dropped messages or adjusting processing speed.

[3] These patterns help ensure that message delivery is prioritized over accommodating individual consumers, thus protecting the integrity of the messaging system.

This means that if a publisher on a connection sends a message to a subject any subscribers on that same connection will receive the message. The NoEcho option can be useful in BUS patterns where all applications subscribe and publish to the same subject. Usually a publish represents a state change that the application already knows about, so in the case where the application publishes an update it does not need to process the update itself. ![](../../../.gitbook/assets/noecho.svg) Keep in mind that each connection will have to turn off echo, and that it is per connection, not per application. The Go client library for NATS will buffer outgoing data to be published when a connection is down, allowing the application to publish messages that would otherwise be sent while the connection is offline. This buffer is part of the library's ability to handle interruptions and ensure messages are sent once the connection is reestablished. When the buffer reaches its maximum size, the application will no longer be able to publish messages and an error will be returned. [3]
